content: Mixed nuts are a type of snack food that consists of a combination of various nuts, either mechanically or manually mixed. Common components of mixed nuts include peanuts (technically a legume), almonds, walnuts, Brazil nuts, cashews, filberts, hazelnuts, and pecans. These nuts may be salted, roasted, cooked, or blanched. Mixed nuts can be consumed directly or used as ingredients in cooking, such as in Tunisian farka, tarts, or toffee. Additionally, they are often included in student food or trail mix, which combines nuts with raisins and other dried ingredients. In Japan, mixed nuts are the second most popular type of nuts, following sweet chestnuts. In the United States, they rank second only to peanuts. U.S. companies sold $783 million worth of mixed nuts containing four or more varieties, primarily in canned form, representing hundreds of millions of pounds. The nuts used in mixed nuts are sourced globally. According to a publication by the Dallas Federal Reserve supporting free trade, this global sourcing incentivizes nut salters to favor free trade policies, unlike nut farmers, who generally support trade barriers. Historically, U.S. nut salters have argued that importing nuts can stimulate domestic production, as mixed nuts create a market platform that benefits the sales of all included varieties. For instance, cashews, which are not grown in North America, must be imported to support the sale of pecans, a nut grown exclusively in North America. Peanuts, being relatively inexpensive, are often a major ingredient in mixed nuts, though they are considered less premium compared to other nuts. Deluxe mixed nuts are frequently marketed as containing no peanuts. For example, Fisher Nuts once had to recall a batch of their deluxe mixed nuts because peanuts were inadvertently included. This recall was not merely a matter of reputation; peanuts are the nut most commonly associated with life-threatening food allergies. Some mixed nut products advertise themselves as containing less than 50% peanuts. In a 1997 segment of 60 Minutes, Andy Rooney tested a 12-ounce can of Planters mixed nuts and found that it contained slightly less than six ounces of peanuts, demonstrating remarkable precision in nut distribution. Besides peanuts, cashews are typically the next least expensive nut and are often the most common ingredient in deluxe mixes. Hazelnuts and Brazil nuts are also relatively inexpensive, while pecans are the most expensive component. The composition of mixed nuts has been regulated by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) since 1977. Before this regulation, the term mixed nuts had no legal definition. A 1964 Consumer Reports investigation of 124 cans of mixed nuts from 31 brands across 17 American cities revealed that most mixed nuts at the time were predominantly peanuts, often comprising 75% of the mix. Peanut-free brands were usually dominated by cashews. Many cans had misleading labels or were underfilled. On March 15, 1977, the FDA established a new standard of identity for mixed nuts. The current standard, as modified in 1993, requires that mixed nuts contain at least four different varieties of tree nuts or peanuts. Products with three or fewer varieties are now commonly labeled as mixes. The container must be at least 85% filled, and the label must specify whether any peanuts are unblanched or of the Spanish variety. The regulations also address weight percentages: if a single variety exceeds 50% of the mix, the label must clearly state contains up to X% [nut type] in 10% increments, up to 80%. For example, the FDA provides the label contains up to 60% pecans as a guideline. To ensure compliance, the FDA samples at least 24 pounds of mixed nuts to minimize sampling error. Descriptive terms like fancy or choice have historically carried no legal meaning in the U.S. and remain absent from current regulations. In a 1915 federal case involving fancy mixed nuts, competitors argued that the product was of inferior quality, but the court declined to accept a trade standard. The term mixed nuts is also used metaphorically to describe a mixture of disparate elements, as seen in the film Mixed Nuts. Additionally, when a container of mixed nuts is shaken and then opened, the larger nuts tend to rise to the top. This phenomenon is known as the Brazil nut effect in the study of granular materials.
